newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sees new Bosnian-Croatian cooperation.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sees new Bosnian-Croatian cooperation.

text.p: The United States on Monday denied envoy Richard Holbrooke's latest Balkans mission was a failure and highlighted what officials called a new spirit of cooperation between the presidents of Bosnia and Croatia.
Asked to comment on suggestions that Holbrooke's weekend trip failed to achieve progress in major areas, State Department spokesman James Rubin said, "I would disagree with that assessment."
But he acknowledged that "in Bosnia, no matter how much progress you make, you still have a long way to go."
"And we have a long way to go," he added.

Holbrooke, architect of the 1995 Dayton peace accords that ended the Bosnia war but are now in serious jeopardy of crumbling, was called back temporarily into government service last week to try to make progress on a number of fronts.
In a television interview later on Monday, Holbrooke acknowledged that the Clinton administration was behind schedule in implementing the Dayton agreements.
"We are a little bit behind schedule in Bosnia, there's no doubt about it. But we are making slow, steady progress," he said on the PBS programme "Newshour With Jim Lehrer."
Holbrooke said Robert Gelbard, permanent U.S. envoy on Bosnia, would return to the region by the end of the week. "I think you will see a real acceleration of effort in the next few months," he said.
Rubin hailed a "spirit of cooperation (that) was new" between Croatian President Franjo Tudjman and Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic and that produced "a series of very concrete commitments."

He said Holbrooke was sent on the mission along with Gelbard to see if they "might wake (Yugoslav) President (Slobodan) Milosevic up to the fact that if he doesn't change gears, if he doesn't start ... seeing that Dayton is implemented, he's going to be left out of Europe."
The United States believes Milosevic has considerable influence on Momcilo Krajisnik and other Bosnian Serb leaders.

The fact that Krajisnik withdrew his opposition to two World Bank loans and made "important concessions on design of the currency coupon, restructuring of the police, getting refugees returned" are "positive steps (and) reinforce the momentum," Rubin said.

Although such issues are important to the peace agreement, top U.S. officials have identified the arrest of indicted war criminals, especially the Bosnian Serbs' wartime leader, Radovan Karadzic, as a priority.
Rubin acknowedged that Milosevic did not promise Holbrooke he would ensure that Karadzic was delivered to the international war crimes tribunal at The Hague.

But Rubin said: "We received commitments that they would try to live up to the (year-old) agreement by which Karadzic will no longer play a role in public life, will not be seen publicly, will not act on behalf of the Bosnian Serb entity."

Reports from Belgrade were that while Holbrooke won a promise that Karadzic would finally disappear from Bosnian politics, the envoy gave Serbian leaders a grace period to remove him to avoid bloodshed. Rubin sidestepped answering a question about a grace period.
